name: Marie Curie
info: Marie Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist who, with Pierre Curie, discovered polonium and radium, coined the word radioactivity, and won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

facts.born: 7 November 1867 in Warsaw, capital of Congress Poland in the Russian Empire, as Maria Salomea Skłodowska, youngest of five children of the teachers Władysław Skłodowski and Bronisława (née Boguska)
facts.died: 4 July 1934 at the Sancellemoz sanatorium in Passy, Haute-Savoie, France, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia believed to have been contracted from long-term exposure to radiation
facts.role: Physicist and chemist; professor at the University of Paris from 1906, the first woman to hold such a post there; director of the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute, Paris (founded 1914); Nobel laureate in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911); director of the Red Cross Radiology Service in the First World War
facts.known: the discovery of polonium and radium with Pierre Curie (1898); the word radioactivity; the isolation of radium; two Nobel Prizes, the first awarded to a woman; mobile X-ray units in the First World War; the Radium Institute in Paris and the Radium Institute in Warsaw

t: Born in Russian-ruled Warsaw, Maria Skłodowska studied at the clandestine Flying University, then in Paris from 1891, where she married Pierre Curie in 1895 and with him announced polonium and radium in 1898.
She won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone, the first person to win a Nobel Prize twice and the first woman to win one.
She met the barriers of her sex and her foreign birth, was vilified by the right-wing press in 1911, and died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia believed to have come from long exposure to radiation.
dyk: The Curies did not patent the process for isolating radium, and Marie Curie insisted that monetary gifts and awards go to the scientific institutions she was affiliated with rather than to her; her papers from the 1890s are still too radioactive to handle without protective clothing.
ev: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, in the Russian Empire
Leaves Poland for Paris and enrols at the University of Paris to study physics, chemistry and mathematics
Announces polonium with Pierre in July and radium in December, and coins the word radioactivity
Awarded her doctorate and, in December, shares the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel
Pierre dies in a road accident; she takes his chair and becomes the first woman professor at the University of Paris
Fails by one or two votes to enter the French Academy of Sciences, and is awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
The Radium Institute is built in Paris; in the war she sets up France's first military radiology centre and mobile X-ray units
Dies of aplastic anaemia at Passy in Haute-Savoie

sections.early:
Maria Salomea Skłodowska, nicknamed Mania, was born on 7 November 1867 in Warsaw, the capital of Congress Poland in the Russian Empire, the fifth and youngest child of the teachers Bronisława (née Boguska) and Władysław Skłodowski. On both sides the family had lost its property through patriotic involvement in Polish national uprisings, the most recent being the January Uprising of 1863–1865, which condemned the next generation to a difficult struggle to get ahead. Władysław taught mathematics and physics and directed two Warsaw gymnasia for boys. After the Russian authorities eliminated laboratory instruction from Polish schools, he brought laboratory equipment home and taught his children to use it; he was later fired for pro-Polish sentiments and forced to take lower-paying posts.

Her mother died of tuberculosis in May 1878, when Maria was ten, and less than three years earlier her oldest sister Zofia had died of typhus contracted from a boarder. Her father was an atheist and her mother a devout Catholic; the deaths led Maria to give up Catholicism and become agnostic. She graduated from a girls' gymnasium on 12 June 1883 with a gold medal. After a collapse, possibly due to depression, she spent a year in the countryside with relatives of her father. Unable to enrol in a regular institution of higher education because she was a woman, she and her sister Bronisława joined the clandestine Flying University, a Polish patriotic institution that admitted women students.
sections.rise:
Maria wished to study in Paris but delayed to help her sister. The two agreed that she would support Bronisława's medical studies there and receive the same help two years later. She worked as a home tutor in Warsaw and then for two years as a governess at Szczuki, with the Żorawski family, relatives of her father, studying in her free time. She fell in love with their son Kazimierz Żorawski, a future mathematician, but his parents rejected the idea of his marrying a penniless relative and he was unable to oppose them. From 1890 to 1891 she began her practical scientific training in a chemistry laboratory at the Museum of Industry and Agriculture in Warsaw, run by her cousin Józef Boguski.

In late 1891 she left for France, where she would be known as Marie, and rented a garret in the Latin Quarter. She studied physics, chemistry and mathematics at the University of Paris on meagre resources, tutoring in the evenings, and was awarded a degree in physics in 1893; with a fellowship she earned a second degree in 1894. She also began work in Gabriel Lippmann's laboratory and investigated the magnetic properties of steels. In 1894 Józef Wierusz-Kowalski introduced her to Pierre Curie, who found her laboratory space. He proposed; she hesitated because she meant to return to Poland, but was refused a place at Kraków University because of sexism in academia, and a letter from Pierre persuaded her to go back to Paris. They married on 26 July 1895 at the Hôtel de Ville in Sceaux, with no religious service.
sections.deeds:
After Röntgen's discovery of X-rays in 1895 and Becquerel's discovery in 1896 that uranium salts emitted penetrating rays, Curie chose uranium rays as a subject for a thesis. Using an electrometer her husband and his brother had developed, she found that the activity of uranium compounds depended only on the quantity of uranium present, and hypothesised that the radiation came from the atom itself, an important step in disproving the assumption that atoms were indivisible. Pitchblende proved four times as active as uranium, which led her to conclude that it contained a more active substance. By 1898 she had found that thorium is also radioactive, and Pierre dropped his work on crystals to join her.

In July 1898 the Curies announced polonium, named for her native Poland, and on 26 December radium. They also coined the word radioactivity. Radium was elusive: it is chemically close to barium, and from a tonne of pitchblende one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride was separated in 1902. In 1910 she isolated pure radium metal. She never succeeded in isolating polonium, whose half-life is only 138 days. Between 1898 and 1902 the Curies published 32 papers. They worked in a converted shed that was poorly ventilated and not waterproof, unaware of the effects of radiation. The Curies did not patent their discovery and benefited little from the radium industry that grew from it.
sections.opponents:
Curie met resistance as a woman and a foreigner. Her paper of 1898 was presented to the Académie des Sciences by Lippmann, as she was not a member, and she was beaten by Gerhard Carl Schmidt in reporting that thorium gives off rays. When the Nobel committee first meant to honour only Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel in 1903, the Swedish mathematician Magnus Gösta Mittag-Leffler alerted Pierre, and after his complaint her name was added. At the Royal Institution in 1903 convention and circumstance meant that Pierre gave the address.

In 1911 the French Academy of Sciences failed by one or two votes to elect her, choosing Édouard Branly instead. The public's attitude tended toward the same xenophobia that had fuelled the Dreyfus affair, which also produced false speculation that she was Jewish, and the right-wing press vilified her as a foreigner and atheist. When it was revealed that year that she had had a year-long affair with the physicist Paul Langevin, a married man estranged from his wife, the tabloids portrayed her as a foreign Jewish home-wrecker, and her academic opponents exploited the scandal. An angry mob gathered in front of her house, and she and her daughters took refuge with her friend Camille Marbo. Svante Arrhenius, chair of the Nobel committee, tried to stop her attending the Chemistry ceremony, citing her moral standing; she replied that there was no relation between her scientific work and her private life. Her daughter later remarked on the French press's hypocrisy in treating her as an unworthy foreigner when she was nominated for a French honour and as a French heroine when she received foreign honours.
sections.last:
During the First World War Curie developed mobile radiography units, known as petites Curies, and set up France's first military radiology centre, operational by late 1914. With her 17-year-old daughter Irène she directed the installation of 20 mobile radiological vehicles and another 200 radiological units at field hospitals in the first year of the war; it is estimated that over a million wounded soldiers were treated with her X-ray units. She never received formal recognition of this from the French government. In 1920 the French government established a stipend for her, and in 1921 she toured the United States to raise funds for radium, and President Warren G. Harding presented her with a gram of radium. She refused the Legion of Honour that the French government offered. From 1922 to 1934 she sat on the League of Nations' International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation. The Radium Institute in Warsaw, with her sister Bronisława as director, opened in 1932.

She visited Poland for the last time in early 1934 and died on 4 July 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia believed to have been contracted from long-term exposure to radiation. She had carried test tubes of radioactive isotopes in her pocket and kept them in her desk drawer, and she was also exposed to X-rays from unshielded equipment in the war. The French office OPRI concluded in 1995 that she could not have been exposed to lethal levels of radium while alive, and speculated that her illness was more likely due to radiography in the war. She was buried at Sceaux beside Pierre; in 1995 their remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris.
sections.legacy:
Curie's work laid the foundation for modern nuclear physics, cancer treatments and radiography. L. Pearce Williams observes that radium's radioactivity seemed to contradict the principle of the conservation of energy and forced a reconsideration of the foundations of physics, and that it gave Ernest Rutherford sources with which to probe the structure of the atom. She founded the Curie Institute in Paris in 1920 and the one in Warsaw in 1932, and the Paris institute, led by her, produced four more Nobel Prize winners, including her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and son-in-law Frédéric Joliot-Curie. She also mentored female scientists there.

She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, the first person to win two, and the only person to win in two scientific fields. In 1995 she became the first woman interred in the Panthéon on her own merits. The curie, a unit of radioactivity, and the element curium are named in her honour, though the commission that chose the unit's name never made clear whether it honoured Pierre, Marie or both. She had been known for her honesty and moderate lifestyle, giving much of her first Nobel Prize money to friends, family, students and research associates; Albert Einstein reportedly remarked that she was probably the only person who could not be corrupted by fame. She taught her daughters Polish and never lost her sense of Polish identity. Her notebooks are expected to remain radioactive for well over a thousand years.

summary: Marie Curie (1867–1934), born in Warsaw and later a French citizen, discovered polonium and radium with Pierre Curie and coined the word radioactivity. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911, founded the Curie Institutes in Paris and Warsaw, and ran mobile X-ray units in the First World War.

notes: Contradiction left out: the 'Early years' section says Bronisława invited Maria to Paris 'at the beginning of 1890' and that she returned to Warsaw 'in early 1889'; the narrative of those years is told without exact dates beyond 1890–1891.

The Radium Institute: the lead says she founded the Curie Institute in Paris in 1920; the text says the Institute was built in 1914 (completed August 1914) and that she was director of the Curie Laboratory in it from 1914. The founding year is given in the legacy as 1920 per the lead; the event for 1914 says 'built'. Another sentence says Warsaw's Radium Institute 'which she had founded in 1932' (lead: 1932); both Warsaw dates agree.
Legion of Honour: the honours list says 'rejected' in 1909; the text places the refusal in 1921. Only the text's 1921 refusal is told.
Event 1903 gives the doctorate (June) and the Nobel Prize (December) together. The 1895 marriage is in the sections but not among the eight events.

The text in the article says Marie was 'four months pregnant' in June 1903; left out. Also left out: the wedding outfit, bicycle trips, the Eusapia Palladino séances, the autochrome photograph, banknotes, coins, films, plays, stamps, Eiffel Tower proposal and the long list of namesakes and awards.
Sancellemoz is given as the article spells it; the 1911 Nobel citation wording differs slightly between lead and text and is not quoted.
